case_info.scenario: A male infant aged 2 weeks presented to an otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarean delivery that was complicated by preeclampsia. Prenatal ultrasonography and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated concern for a tongue cyst. At birth, a small midline tongue defect was noted, for which the patient was referred to an ear, nose, and throat clinic. At the time of the initial evaluation, he was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. He was found to have a shallow, midline tongue depression with no discrete masses or lesions. Recommendations were for a watchful waiting approach to allow for granulation of the defect. The patient presented for follow-up approximately 2 years later, with his parents reporting concerns for persistence of the lesion. He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. Following surgical excision, histopathologic examination of the excised tract demonstrated squamous and respiratory mucosa with regional striated muscle bundles, smooth muscle, adipose tissue, and minor salivary glands.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.

  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

case_info.scenario: A male infant aged 2 weeks presented to an otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarean delivery that was complicated by preeclampsia. Prenatal ultrasonography and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated concern for a tongue cyst. At birth, a small midline tongue defect was noted, for which the patient was referred to an ear, nose, and throat clinic. At the time of the initial evaluation, he was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. He was found to have a shallow, midline tongue depression with no discrete masses or lesions. Recommendations were for a watchful waiting approach to allow for granulation of the defect. The patient presented for follow-up approximately 2 years later, with his parents reporting concerns for persistence of the lesion. He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. Following surgical excision, histopathologic examination of the excised tract demonstrated squamous and respiratory mucosa with regional striated muscle bundles, smooth muscle, adipose tissue, and minor salivary glands.

case_info.explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.
